\section[fuga, fugae]{fuga, fugae — flight, running away}

\label{lesson:LA-C322-fuga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an uproar, then the Latin for a shout.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fuga, fugae}
\textbf{fuga, fugae} — \textquotedblleft{}flight, running away\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hostēs sē in fugam dedērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The enemy took to flight.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, from \emph{fugiō} (taught). \emph{In fugam dare}: to put to flight.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fuga} belongs with \emph{fugiō}, \textquotedblleft{}to flee\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), and matches Greek \emph{phygē}, \textquotedblleft{}flight\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{fugitive} comes from the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fuga, fugae}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fuga, fugae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fuga, fugae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for an uproar, then the Latin for a shout, then say \emph{fuga, fugae} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[effugiō, effugere]{effugiō, effugere — to escape}

\label{lesson:LA-C322-effugio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a shout, then the Latin for flight.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: effugiō, effugere}
\textbf{effugiō, effugere} — \textquotedblleft{}to escape\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Paucī ex incendiō effūgērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Few escaped from the fire.}
\end{quote}

\emph{effugiō, effugere, effūgī}: \emph{ex} + \emph{fugiō}, also with the accusative: \emph{perīculum effugere}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{effugiō} is built on \emph{fugiō}, \textquotedblleft{}to flee\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ex-}, \textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to flee out of danger.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{effugiō, effugere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{effugiō, effugere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a shout, then the Latin for flight, then say \emph{effugiō, effugere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[ēvādō, ēvādere]{ēvādō, ēvādere — to get away, to come out}

\label{lesson:LA-C322-evado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for flight, then the Latin for to escape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ēvādō, ēvādere}
\textbf{ēvādō, ēvādere} — \textquotedblleft{}to get away, to come out\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nauta ex undīs ad lītus ēvāsit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The sailor got out of the waves to the shore.}
\end{quote}

\emph{ēvādō, ēvādere, ēvāsī, ēvāsum}: \emph{ē} + \emph{vādō}, 'to go'. English \emph{evade}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ēvādō} is built on \emph{vādō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go, to rush\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ex-}, \textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB). English \emph{evade} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for flight, then the Latin for to escape, then say \emph{ēvādō, ēvādere} again

\section[pereō, perīre]{pereō, perīre — to perish, to die; to be lost}

\label{lesson:LA-C322-pereo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to escape, then the Latin for to get away.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: pereō, perīre}
\textbf{pereō, perīre} — \textquotedblleft{}to perish, to die; to be lost\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
In illō incendiō multī periērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Many died in that fire.}
\end{quote}

\emph{pereō, perīre, periī, peritum}, like \emph{eō} (taught). In comedy a slave cries \emph{periī!}, 'I am done for!'

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pereō} is built on \emph{eō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{per-}, here \textquotedblleft{}to destruction\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to go to ruin. English \emph{perish} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pereō, perīre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{pereō, perīre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to escape, then the Latin for to get away, then say \emph{pereō, perīre} again

\section[custōs, custōdis]{custōs, custōdis — a guard, a keeper}

\label{lesson:LA-C322-custos}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to get away, then the Latin for to perish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: custōs, custōdis}
\textbf{custōs, custōdis} — \textquotedblleft{}a guard, a keeper\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Custōdēs portae dormiēbant, et fūr intrāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The guards of the gate were asleep, and the thief got in.}
\end{quote}

Masculine or feminine, 3rd declension. A satirist asked who would guard the guards themselves. English \emph{custody} is of its family.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{custōs} is linked by Lewis \& Short with a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to cover, to hide\textquotedblright{}; the link is not certain. English \emph{custody} comes from its family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\section[(dialogue)]{Words from chapters 315–322 — a review}

\label{lesson:LA-R322-review-315-322}



\begin{quote}
Say the Latin for a shipwreck and shipwrecked.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a shipwreck, shipwrecked, to sink, to overwhelm, a disaster
  \item to snatch away, unharmed, to come to help, to run to help, help
  \item a fire, heat, glowing ash, a firebrand, burning heat
  \item to burn up, to burn, to blaze, to smoke, to go up in flames
  \item a fire pump, a fire bucket, to put out, the watch, to scorch
  \item panic, fear, dread, frightened, to panic
  \item threats, to threaten, to frighten, an uproar, a shout
  \item flight, to escape, to get away, to perish, a guard
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A shipwreck? (\textbf{naufragium, naufragiī}.) Shipwrecked? (\textbf{naufragus, naufraga, naufragum}.) To sink? (\textbf{mergō, mergere}.) To overwhelm? (\textbf{obruō, obruere}.) A disaster? (\textbf{calamitās, calamitātis}.) To snatch away? (\textbf{ēripiō, ēripere}.) Unharmed? (\textbf{incolumis, incolume}.) To come to help? (\textbf{subveniō, subvenīre}.) To run to help? (\textbf{succurrō, succurrere}.) Help? (\textbf{auxilium, auxiliī}.) A fire? (\textbf{incendium, incendiī}.) Heat? (\textbf{aestus, aestūs}.) Glowing ash? (\textbf{favilla, favillae}.) A firebrand? (\textbf{torris, torris}.) Burning heat? (\textbf{ārdor, ārdōris}.) To burn up? (\textbf{cremō, cremāre}.) To burn? (\textbf{ūrō, ūrere}.) To blaze? (\textbf{flagrō, flagrāre}.) To smoke? (\textbf{fūmō, fūmāre}.) To go up in flames? (\textbf{cōnflagrō, cōnflagrāre}.) A fire pump? (\textbf{sīphō, sīphōnis}.) A fire bucket? (\textbf{hama, hamae}.) To put out? (\textbf{restinguō, restinguere}.) The watch? (\textbf{excubiae, excubiārum}.) To scorch? (\textbf{ambūrō, ambūrere}.) Panic? (\textbf{pavor, pavōris}.) Fear? (\textbf{metus, metūs}.) Dread? (\textbf{formīdō, formīdinis}.) Frightened? (\textbf{pavidus, pavida, pavidum}.) To panic? (\textbf{trepidō, trepidāre}.) Threats? (\textbf{minae, minārum}.) To threaten? (\textbf{minitor, minitārī}.) To frighten? (\textbf{terreō, terrēre}.) An uproar? (\textbf{tumultus, tumultūs}.) A shout? (\textbf{clāmor, clāmōris}.) Flight? (\textbf{fuga, fugae}.) To escape? (\textbf{effugiō, effugere}.) To get away? (\textbf{ēvādō, ēvādere}.) To perish? (\textbf{pereō, perīre}.) A guard? (\textbf{custōs, custōdis}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
